name: Treaty with the Menominee, 1856
promises: Article 1: the Menominee ceded not more than two townships in the western part of their reservation, for the Stockbridge and Munsee and other New York Indians.
Article 2: the United States to pay sixty cents an acre, if the New York Indians were located there, to be spent on Menominee improvement as under the 1854 treaty.
Article 3: roads laid out by law to have right of way through Menominee lands on the same terms as through citizens' lands; annuities might be paid semi-annually or quarterly.
compensation: The treaty price was sixty cents an acre. Whether it was paid was not traced.
today: Royce records that the Stockbridge and Munsee were moved onto the two townships, and that by Act of February 6, 1871 they sold all but 18 sections of it (Royce p. 817). No court, claims-commission or government finding of a breach of this treaty was found.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe publishes the text of the 1856 treaty among its treaty pages, without commentary.

sources.title: Treaty with the Menominee, 1856 (Kappler vol. 2, p. 755)

sources.title: Charles C. Royce, Indian Land Cessions in the United States (18th Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899), schedule pp. 816-817

openQuestions: Searches of the Oklahoma State University Indian Claims Commission collection for "Menominee" returned no decisions, so Menominee dockets could not be read there; a Menominee claim over the 1856 price may exist elsewhere.
Menominee Tribe v. United States, 117 Ct. Cl. 442 (1950) concerns timber cutting under the 1908 Act, not this cession.
treaties.json links Royce p. 854 for this entry; the Menominee entry of February 11, 1856 is on Royce pp. 816-817 (area 403). Not edited.

Audit 2026-11-08: ratified (April 18, 1856) and proclaimed (April 24, 1856) dates added from the Oklahoma State University Kappler text. The Menominee Court of Claims opinions under the 1935 jurisdictional act (95 Ct. Cl. 232, 101 Ct. Cl. 10 and 22, 102 Ct. Cl. 555, 107 Ct. Cl. 23, 117 Ct. Cl. 442) were opened at the Caselaw Access Project; none concerns the 1856 cession or its price.
